title: Fatigue, a facial rash, and frothy urine
presentation: A 24-year-old woman is referred from her family doctor with three months of fatigue and pain in her hands and wrists, a rash on her cheeks that flares after sun exposure, and two weeks of ankle swelling and frothy urine. Triage: BP 148/92, T 37.4 C, HR 88. Urine dipstick: protein 3+, blood 2+.

stages.label: History
stages.text: Her joint pain is symmetrical, involves the MCPs, PIPs, and wrists, and comes with about an hour of morning stiffness; there is no swelling she has noticed and no deformity. The cheek rash spares the folds beside her nose and appeared after a beach holiday. She has had painless ulcers on the roof of her mouth, is losing more hair than usual, and her fingers turn white then blue in the cold. No fever, no pleuritic chest pain, no sore throat or skin infection in the preceding weeks, no diarrhoea. No previous kidney problems. Medications: a combined oral contraceptive pill; occasional ibuprofen for the joints (none in the last month). No hydralazine, minocycline, or other new drugs. An aunt has 'lupus'. She has never been pregnant.
stages.prompt: What is your leading diagnosis, what else is on the differential, and what does the dipstick oblige you to do today?
stages.learner_goal: Name systemic lupus erythematosus, keep post-infectious GN, IgA nephropathy, RA, and drug-induced lupus in view, and recognise that proteinuria with haematuria means the kidney must be characterised now.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: BP 150/94. Erythema over both malar eminences and the bridge of the nose, sparing the nasolabial folds. Two painless ulcers on the hard palate. Diffuse, non-scarring thinning of scalp hair. Tender synovitis of the second and third MCPs and both wrists, no deformity, no nodules. Bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-shin. Chest clear, no pleural or pericardial rub, no murmur. No lymphadenopathy, no splenomegaly. Neurological examination normal.
stages.prompt: Which tests separate the diagnoses on your list, and which urine tests matter most? Tell me what you expect each to show if this is lupus.
stages.learner_goal: Order urine microscopy for an active sediment and a quantified protein-creatinine ratio, ANA with anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, and complements, a blood count, and antiphospholipid antibodies.

available_tests.urine microscopy: Urine microscopy: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, granular casts
available_tests.urine protein creatinine ratio: Spot UPCR 3.8 g/g (24-hour collection estimate 3.5 g/day)
available_tests.creatinine: Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (115 micromol/L), eGFR 58; urea 9.5 mmol/L
available_tests.direct coombs: Direct antiglobulin test positive; reticulocytes mildly raised; haptoglobin low-normal
available_tests.ena: Anti-Smith positive; anti-RNP positive; anti-Ro negative; anti-La negative
available_tests.complement: C3 0.42 g/L (low; reference 0.9-1.8), C4 0.06 g/L (low; reference 0.1-0.4)
available_tests.antiphospholipid antibodies: Lupus anticoagulant negative; anticardiolipin IgG 25 GPL (low positive); anti-beta2-glycoprotein I negative
available_tests.rheumatoid factor and ccp: RF weakly positive 22 IU/mL, anti-CCP negative
available_tests.aso titre: ASO titre normal; throat swab negative
available_tests.renal ultrasound: Normal-sized kidneys with mildly increased echogenicity, no obstruction
available_tests.hand x-rays: No erosions, no joint space narrowing

stages.label: Results
stages.text: Urine microscopy: dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts. UPCR 3.8 g/g. Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (eGFR 58), albumin 26 g/L. Hb 9.8 g/dL, WBC 3.1 with lymphocytes 0.7, platelets 118, direct Coombs positive. ANA 1:1280 homogeneous. Anti-dsDNA 420 IU/mL. Anti-Smith positive, anti-RNP positive. C3 0.42 g/L, C4 0.06 g/L (both low). Lupus anticoagulant negative, anticardiolipin IgG low positive. ESR 72, CRP 6. Anti-CCP negative, hand films without erosions. ASO normal, ANCA negative, viral serology negative. Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys.
stages.prompt: Interpret the serology for me: what do the anti-dsDNA and the complements tell you about disease activity and the kidney? Then tell me what you still need before you can choose therapy, and why you cannot skip it.
stages.learner_goal: Explain that high anti-dsDNA with low C3 and C4 indicates immune-complex-mediated active disease and tracks with nephritis, and insist on a renal biopsy because histological class determines treatment.

stages.label: Renal biopsy
stages.text: Renal biopsy (22 glomeruli): diffuse endocapillary proliferation involving 60% of glomeruli, with two cellular crescents and segmental fibrinoid necrosis; subendothelial 'wire-loop' deposits. Immunofluorescence: granular capillary-wall and mesangial staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q ('full house'). Electron microscopy: subendothelial and mesangial electron-dense deposits. Modified NIH activity index 10/24, chronicity index 2/12. Interpretation: ISN/RPS class IV (diffuse) lupus nephritis, active lesions, minimal chronicity.
stages.prompt: Final diagnosis and a complete management plan: induction, the drug every lupus patient should be on, blood pressure and proteinuria, her contraceptive pill, and what you will monitor.
stages.learner_goal: Commit to class IV lupus nephritis and lay out induction immunosuppression with glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, renin-angiotensin blockade, withdrawal of oestrogen, and a monitoring plan.

diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with class IV (diffuse proliferative) lupus nephritis
key_clues: Young woman with photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia, and symmetrical non-erosive synovitis
Leukopenia with lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and Coombs-positive anaemia
ANA 1:1280 with anti-dsDNA 420 IU/mL and anti-Smith positive
Low C3 and C4 indicating complement consumption by immune complexes
Active urinary sediment (dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts) with nephrotic-range proteinuria and reduced eGFR
Full-house immunofluorescence and diffuse endocapillary proliferation on biopsy
High ESR with near-normal CRP, typical of lupus activity without infection or serositis

distractors.name: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
distractors.why_not: No preceding pharyngitis or impetigo, ASO normal, and three months of multisystem symptoms with anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith positivity; post-infectious GN does not produce full-house immunofluorescence.

distractors.name: IgA nephropathy
distractors.why_not: No synpharyngitic haematuria; serology, cytopenias, and rash point elsewhere, and immunofluorescence shows IgG-dominant full-house staining with C1q rather than IgA dominance.

distractors.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
distractors.why_not: The arthritis is non-erosive with negative anti-CCP; RA does not cause malar rash, oral ulcers, cytopenias, hypocomplementaemia, or proliferative glomerulonephritis. A weakly positive RF is common in lupus.

distractors.name: Mixed connective tissue disease
distractors.why_not: Anti-RNP is positive but so are anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith, and diffuse proliferative nephritis with low complements is characteristic of SLE rather than MCTD.

distractors.name: Drug-induced lupus
distractors.why_not: No hydralazine, procainamide, minocycline, or anti-TNF exposure; drug-induced lupus rarely involves the kidney and does not produce anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith antibodies.

distractors.name: Primary nephrotic syndrome (minimal change or membranous)
distractors.why_not: The sediment is active with red cell casts and complements are low; a bland nephrotic picture would not have haematuria or hypocomplementaemia.

rubric.description: Names systemic lupus erythematosus at the history stage
rubric.concept: Photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, alopecia, and non-erosive arthritis in a young woman is SLE until proven otherwise

rubric.description: Recognises proteinuria with haematuria as glomerulonephritis needing urgent characterisation
rubric.concept: Proteinuria with haematuria in a lupus patient means nephritis until proven otherwise; delay costs nephrons

rubric.description: Orders urine microscopy for sediment and a quantified protein-creatinine ratio (or 24-hour protein)
rubric.concept: Urine sediment and quantified proteinuria are the screening tests for lupus nephritis; a dipstick is not enough

rubric.description: Orders ANA with anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith (ENA), and complements C3/C4
rubric.concept: ANA is the screen (sensitive, not specific); anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific; C3/C4 and anti-dsDNA are the activity markers

rubric.description: Interprets low C3/C4 with high anti-dsDNA as immune complex activity correlating with active nephritis
rubric.concept: Anti-dsDNA rises and complements fall as immune complexes form and deposit; together they predict and track renal flares

rubric.description: Requests a renal biopsy before choosing therapy, because histological class determines treatment
rubric.concept: Any lupus patient with proteinuria above 0.5 g/day or an active sediment needs a renal biopsy; class cannot be inferred from serology

rubric.description: Final diagnosis is lupus nephritis (ideally class IV / diffuse proliferative)
Chooses induction with mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids, with or without belimumab or voclosporin
rubric.concept: Class III/IV induction: MMF or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids, adding belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor; maintenance with MMF or azathioprine

rubric.description: Adds hydroxychloroquine, renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuria and blood pressure, and stops the oestrogen-containing pill
rubric.concept: Every lupus patient gets hydroxychloroquine; proteinuria gets an ACE inhibitor or ARB; oestrogen is withdrawn in active nephritis and antiphospholipid positivity, with safe contraception on teratogenic drugs

management_summary: She has SLE with active class IV lupus nephritis (activity index 10, chronicity 2), so treat promptly to preserve nephrons. Induction: intravenous methylprednisolone 250-500 mg daily for three days, then oral prednisolone around 0.5 mg/kg with a taper to 5 mg or less by six months, combined with mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 g/day (or low-dose Euro-Lupus intravenous cyclophosphamide, 500 mg every two weeks for six doses), and consider adding belimumab or voclosporin as current guidelines favour triple therapy. Start hydroxychloroquine for everyone. Start an ACE inhibitor or ARB and target blood pressure below 130/80. Stop the combined oral contraceptive (active nephritis plus a positive anticardiolipin) and offer a progestogen-only or intrauterine method; counsel that mycophenolate is teratogenic and pregnancy should be deferred until disease is quiet for six months. Check TPMT if azathioprine is planned for maintenance, vaccinate (pneumococcal, influenza, HPV), give bone protection, and consider Pneumocystis prophylaxis during high-dose steroids. Monitor UPCR, creatinine, blood count, anti-dsDNA, and complements every four to six weeks; the target is a UPCR below 0.5 g/g by 12 months.
teaching_points: Serology has two jobs. ANA screens (99% sensitive, poorly specific); anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith confirm (specific); and anti-dsDNA with C3 and C4 track activity. High anti-dsDNA with low complements means immune complexes are forming and depositing, and the kidney is the organ most likely to be paying for it.

Lupus nephritis is diagnosed under the microscope, not in the serum. Any lupus patient with proteinuria above 0.5 g/day, an active sediment, or an unexplained rise in creatinine needs a renal biopsy, because class II, III/IV, and V are treated differently and the activity and chronicity indices set the prognosis.

Proliferative nephritis (class III/IV) needs induction immunosuppression now: mycophenolate or low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids, increasingly with belimumab or voclosporin added, followed by years of maintenance. The dose of steroid is falling in every successive guideline.

The non-negotiables for every lupus patient: hydroxychloroquine, sun protection, blood pressure and proteinuria control with renin-angiotensin blockade, contraception and pregnancy planning on teratogenic drugs, no oestrogen with antiphospholipid antibodies or active nephritis, and vaccination before immunosuppression.
